hero.description: A cluttered backlog column of abstract ticket cards. Our ticket is red and flagged bug. As scrolling begins it lifts out of the column onto the track. Cards carry no IDs, titles, names, avatars, or PR number. The only card text is 'bug' and the Illustration tag. The hero.visualLabel sits beside the column as real text.

sixty.description: The track pauses. The ticket sits beside the summary like a ticket detail panel. The panel shows only this section's real text and the Illustration tag: no ID, key, title, assignee, reporter, sprint, priority, avatar, or other person field.

pipeline.description: One station per step. Reproduce, Fix, Verify (second agent marker with a fresh context badge), Regression, Review, Opened PR (ticket becomes a PR card). The PR card has no PR number, branch, repo, author, or avatar; before and after thumbnails are abstract shapes, never video or app images.

safety.description: The track passes a gate. A billing / auth lane stops at a human-approval checkpoint, a single retry meter fills to a cap line, and the drawn kill switch is the real control. The retry meter is one continuous bar with no discrete units, numbers, tier names, or tier count, so no cap or tier count can be read from it.

mcp.description: The track branches into tool lanes. A classifier node routes a question to one lane. A delete lane is visibly fenced off.

platform.description: The track runs through a calm grid of abstract component tiles. Small markers join the track behind the ticket to show team adoption. Markers have no initials or avatars; their count is decorative and never equals a team size stated on the site (3, 5, 9, or 35).

independent.description: Two side tracks branch off to the FoundrKids and Pocket Chronicle panels and rejoin.

career.description: The track becomes a vertical commit log. Each role is a commit with date range and title. Older commits are dimmer.

ask.description: A terminal-styled panel beside the track.

recommendations.description: Only rendered when recommendations.enabled is true. Signed-commit style quotes as real HTML text.

contact.description: The PR's checks pass, it merges, and its status light turns green. The glow lands on the contact CTAs. Ready for review. The PR card carries no PR number, IDs, titles, names, or avatars. Its only text is the merged status and the Illustration tag.

titleLine.text: Senior Full Stack Engineer | Agentic Engineering

focus.text: 15+ years shipping production systems end to end, specializing in agentic engineering with real guardrails.

achievements.text: Sole author of an agentic engineering system at Atlas UP: 30+ chained Claude Code skills that took Jira tickets from reproduction through fix, verification, regression, and code review.
Used that system to clear a backlog of 100+ bugs and ship about 25 features in about six weeks, with roughly 95% of bug tickets accepted on first pass by code review and QA.

Designed the safety model: a separate agent verified every fix with fresh context, retries were capped by risk tier, billing and auth always stopped for a human, and a global kill switch paused all loops.

Core contributor on EOS One's production MCP server, helping build the question classifier and tool layer that let customers connect Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok to their data, with destructive actions kept in the app and never exposed to LLMs.

Owned the AI-powered Accountability Chart and V/TO builders for EOS One end to end, from Python microservices and LLM integration through the frontend; the Accountability Chart builder became the platform's most used AI tool across roughly 10,000 monthly active users.

intro.text: At Atlas UP I was the sole author of an agentic engineering system: 30+ chained Claude Code skills that took Jira tickets from reproduction through fix, verification, regression, and code review, ending in an opened pull request.

visualNote.text: The ticket, track, and stations are original drawings. No real tickets, code, prompts, or screenshots appear here.

stages.label: Reproduce
stages.text: The loop started by reproducing the ticket.

aside.label: Related: knowledge base
aside.text: The agents drove the app from a persistent knowledge base I built, and a nightly consolidation process pruned contradictions and duplicate lessons learned.

stages.label: Fix
stages.text: Next, the loop made the fix.

stages.label: Verify
stages.text: A separate agent, not the one that wrote the fix, verified every fix with fresh context.

stages.label: Regression
stages.text: The change then ran through regression.

aside.label: Related: release regression
aside.text: At the release level, I built an AI regression lane that ran TestRail cases through Claude Code and Playwright, scoped to each release's blast radius. It cut regression cycles from about a week to 8 to 12 hours and removed QA as the release bottleneck.

aside.label: Related: PR review agent
aside.text: I also built an autonomous pull request review agent that scanned Azure DevOps hourly and reviewed every PR for six weeks, hundreds in total. It ranked findings by severity and posted fix suggestions directly on each PR.

stages.label: Opened PR
stages.text: The loop ended with an opened pull request that included before and after videos.

result.text: I used the system to clear a backlog of 100+ bugs and ship about 25 features in about six weeks, with roughly 95% of bug tickets accepted on first pass by code review and QA.

intro.text: I was a core contributor on the team that built a production MCP server for EOS One. It let customers connect Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok to their EOS One data.

classifier.text: I helped build the question classifier and tool layer. The classifier routed each request to the right tool.

destructive.text: Destructive actions, like deletes, were deliberately excluded, so they had to happen in the app, never through an LLM.

ownership.text: I built and owned the design system for EOS One, an AI business operating system, then expanded into full stack AI work, shipping LLM features used by about 10,000 monthly active users.

aiBuilders.text: At Atlas UP I owned the AI-powered Accountability Chart and V/TO builders end to end, from Python microservices and LLM integration through the frontend. The Accountability Chart builder became the platform's most used AI tool across roughly 10,000 monthly active users.

llmArchitecture.text: As one of three staff engineers, I co-designed the LLM and chatbot architecture, establishing the patterns for AI features across the platform.

library.text: At EOS Worldwide I architected and built the EOS One component library from the ground up: about 150 components, frontend services, and a design-token-based styling system that set the architecture, patterns, and standards the product still runs on. After the acquisition I continued to own and extend it.

stack.text: I contributed across a C#, .NET, SignalR, Redis, and Cosmos DB stack and Python LLM microservices.

voiceNotes.text: At EOS Worldwide I built voice-activated note taking for EOS One's real-time SignalR meetings, backed by a Python microservice that recorded sessions, generated notes, emailed summaries afterward, and suggested to-dos for each team member.

testing.text: At EOS Worldwide I led frontend unit testing with Vitest and CI/CD quality gates, bringing frontend services to about 85% test coverage.

shipping.text: At Atlas UP we ran a weekly release train and used Ship/Show/Ask, so changes reached production almost daily on Azure DevOps Pipelines.

review.text: At EOS Worldwide, as one of three senior engineers on a predominantly junior team, I personally reviewed every frontend pull request and mentored four to five junior developers who were on track for senior roles by the end of their tenure.

mentoring.text: After my promotion to Staff Front End Engineer there, I managed three direct reports through one on ones and growth planning while staying hands-on in delivery.

mentorship.text: I have a track record of mentoring junior engineers toward senior roles.

adoption.text: At Atlas UP, I led the team's AI adoption from light Cursor use to Claude Code, prompt engineering, and ultimately autonomous agent loops and harness engineering. Teammates adopted the skills I wrote after seeing my delivery rate climb.

standards.text: At Atlas UP, I encoded team standards into the PR review agent described in The Pipeline.

retention.text: I was retained as one of three staff engineers when the post-acquisition team went from 35 people to 9.

intro.text: I build AI products on my own: FoundrKids, an AI and entrepreneurship learning platform in pre-launch; Pocket Chronicle, a native iOS app I shipped to the App Store and later retired; RoleHawk, a free, open source AI job search copilot; and this site, with its RAG assistant.

summary.text: An AI and entrepreneurship learning platform for kids 8 to 15, where an AI coach guides kids through building missions while parents track safety.

points.text: I built the full stack solo: three Vue apps, a FastAPI backend, Postgres with pgvector, Redis, and Stripe on Fly.io and Neon, plus an adaptive learning engine backed by about 2,500 tests.

I designed a six-layer safety model for every model call: blocklist, OpenAI moderation, prompt scaffolding, the model, a streaming sentence buffer, and a PII-redacting output filter. It fails closed, ending the session and alerting the parent on critical events.
Cost-controlled model routing sends work to Anthropic or OpenAI by mission tier, with cross-vendor failover and a monthly spend cap per household.
COPPA is built into the data layer: verified parental consent, a 90-day chat purge, real child deletion, and a tamper-proof audit log.

name.note: The resume (L62) and HEADLINE_PROOF spell this with a trailing s. That is a typo; always use the singular.

status.text: Shipped to the App Store in 2026, now retired. It worked end to end but did not find users, so I shut it down rather than keep paying to run the backend.

summary.text: A native iOS family memory app I shipped solo, from concept to the App Store in about a month, by directing AI agents outside my primary stack.

points.text: Built with SwiftUI, SwiftData with offline sync, StoreKit 2, Sign in with Apple, and on-device transcription and Foundation Models, backed by an async FastAPI and SQLAlchemy service on Postgres, deployed to Fly.io.
About 2,700 automated tests and 200 merged PRs, with written specs and decision logs behind every change.

summary.text: A local-first AI job search copilot that takes users from resume to offer.

points.text: I built the full stack solo: React 18, TypeScript, and TanStack Query on the frontend; Python FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, SQLite, and Playwright on the backend; shipped as a one-line installer for macOS, Windows, and Linux.
Anti-hallucination guardrails: tailored CVs and cover letters pull facts only from the user's profile, then a fact checker and a separate AI review verify them.
Models are routed by cost, with Haiku for ranking and Opus for writing, plus a monthly spend cap and cost estimates shown before each batch runs.
Private by design: it runs only on localhost, keeps API keys in the OS keychain, sends no telemetry, and treats job postings as untrusted input to block prompt injection.

summary.text: My Next.js, React, and TypeScript resume site, with a RAG assistant that answers questions about my work.

points.text: The Ask assistant retrieves the top 8 matches from Cloudflare Vectorize, and Claude returns structured JSON with a grounded flag, handing off to email when the sources don't support an answer.
A TypeScript Cloudflare Worker proxy keeps API keys out of the browser, with Turnstile, an origin allow list, rate limits, and a daily spend cap.

It is a static Next.js 15 and React 19 export deployed to GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions, with GSAP and Lenis scroll animations, reduced-motion support, a motion pause switch, and a 100 Lighthouse accessibility score.
